about: Lesson 8 (Who runs, and what sets the price?): Prairie Town's five plants offer their power at their running cost in one hour of lesson 0's real day; the operator stacks the offers cheapest first and the last plant needed sets the price for everyone (a uniform-price market). The hour's demand, wind and solar are cut from town_year.json exactly as lesson 0 does (town.json, scenario lesson0). Gas plants' running cost = heat rate x gas price + other running costs; at the reference gas price this gives lesson 0's $40 and $100 per MWh. All Prairie Town numbers are illustrative.

gas.note: $6.00/MMBtu is Prairie Town's illustrative reference, the price behind lesson 0's costs. Marks: average cost of natural gas to U.S. power plants (EIA, Electric Power Annual, Table 7.4, final data).

cc.note: Illustrative. A new combined-cycle plant needs about 6.2 MMBtu per MWh (EIA AEO2026).

peaker.note: Illustrative: an old, inefficient peaker. A new combustion turbine needs about 9.1 MMBtu per MWh (EIA AEO2026).

credit.note: Illustrative: a payment per MWh produced, so the wind farm still earns at prices down to minus the credit.

inflexible.note: Illustrative: the price the plant would accept rather than stop and restart later.

eia-2012-negative.text: EIA, Today in Energy: Negative wholesale electricity prices occur in RTOs
